lead: A curved beam is a member whose centreline is an arc: a crane hook, a C-frame, a chain link. Bending stress in it is not linear across the depth. The neutral axis moves toward the centre of curvature, so the inner fibre sees the highest stress. This chapter derives the rectangular-section formula, shows the hyperbolic stress distribution, and applies it to a crane hook. Use it whenever the depth is not small compared with the radius; the straight-beam formula then under-predicts the inner stress.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for bending stress and Chapter 1.7 for adding direct stress to bending stress.

blocks.text: In a straight beam, a fibre at distance y from the neutral axis has length proportional to y. Strain changes linearly with y, so stress changes linearly. In a curved beam, a fibre at radius r has length r dθ. For the same rotation of the section, the change in length depends on r in a different way. The strain is not linear in r.

The neutral axis is the radius where bending stress is zero. For pure bending with no axial force, the sum of forces across the section must be zero. Because inner fibres are shorter, the neutral axis shifts inward, toward the centre of curvature. It lies at R<sub>n</sub>, which is less than the centroidal radius R.

blocks.where: R<sub>i</sub> is inner radius (mm); R<sub>o</sub> is outer radius (mm); h is depth (mm); ln is natural log. For a rectangular section, A = b h.
R = R<sub>i</sub> + h/2 is the centroidal radius (mm); e is the shift of the neutral axis from the centroid (mm).

blocks.text: The bending stress at radius r is hyperbolic, not linear. Take M positive when it tends to open the curve, the usual crane-hook case. Positive stress means tension. With the opposite sign convention, reverse every sign.

blocks.where: σ is bending stress at radius r (MPa or N/mm²); M is bending moment (N·mm); A is area (mm²); e is neutral-axis shift (mm); r is the radius to the point (mm).

blocks.text: At the inner fibre, r = R<sub>i</sub> < R<sub>n</sub>, so the term (R<sub>n</sub> − r) is positive and large. The small r in the denominator also raises the stress. The inner fibre therefore has the highest bending stress. Add direct stress separately: σ<sub>total</sub> = P/A + σ, where P is axial force (N, tension positive).

A crane hook is a curved beam with a load P hanging from its lower end. The critical section is usually the horizontal section through the hook where the load line passes near the centre of curvature. If the load line passes through the centre, the moment about the centroid is M = P R. Here P is in newtons and R is the centroidal radius in millimetres, so M is in N·mm.

The load opens the hook. The inner fibre is in tension from bending. Direct stress P/A is also tensile. The two add at the inner fibre and give the maximum tensile stress. At the outer fibre, bending gives compression; the direct tension reduces its magnitude. Check the outer fibre separately for the maximum compressive stress.

A C-frame under load works the same way. The inner corner of the C is the high-stress fibre. Use the curved-beam formula when the depth h is comparable with R. When h is much smaller than R, e and Rn approach straight-beam values, and the straight formula from Chapter 1.6 is close enough. Stress concentration at the inner fibre and fatigue of hooks are covered in Unit 2.

Follow four checks. First, find R<sub>o</sub> = R<sub>i</sub> + h, A = b h, and R = R<sub>i</sub> + h/2. Second, compute R<sub>n</sub> and e. Third, compute M from the load and its lever arm about the centroid. Fourth, compute bending stress at the inner and outer fibres, then add direct stress with the correct sign.

items: Use R<sub>n</sub>, not R, in the stress formula.
Use the radius r to the fibre, not the diameter.
Keep M in N·mm and lengths in mm so stress comes out in N/mm² (MPa).
Check both fibres; the larger magnitude may be compressive.

figure.caption: Stress across the 30 mm × 60 mm hook section of the worked example. The inner fibre reaches about 121 MPa tension; the straight-beam line would give only about 89 MPa there.

spec.aria: Curved-beam stress is highest at the inner fibre and falls hyperbolically; the straight-beam line is linear and under-predicts the inner stress.

examples.question: A crane hook carries 20 kN. Its cross-section is rectangular: width 30 mm, depth 60 mm. The inner radius is 40 mm. Find the maximum tensile stress at the inner fibre and the maximum compressive stress at the outer fibre using curved-beam theory.
steps: Outer radius: R<sub>o</sub> = R<sub>i</sub> + h = 40 mm + 60 mm = 100 mm.
Area: A = b h = 30 mm × 60 mm = 1800 mm².
Centroidal radius: R = R<sub>i</sub> + h/2 = 40 mm + 30 mm = 70 mm.
Neutral-axis radius: R<sub>n</sub> = h / ln(R<sub>o</sub>/R<sub>i</sub>) = 60 / ln(100/40) = 60 / 0.9163 = 65.48 mm.
Neutral-axis shift: e = R − R<sub>n</sub> = 70 mm − 65.48 mm = 4.52 mm.
Load line through the centre of curvature: M = P R = 20,000 N × 70 mm = 1,400,000 N·mm.
Direct stress: P/A = 20,000 N / 1800 mm² = 11.11 MPa tension.
Inner fibre, r = 40 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = M(R<sub>n</sub> − r)/(A e r) = 1,400,000 × (65.48 − 40) / (1800 × 4.52 × 40) = 109.65 MPa. Total σ<sub>inner</sub> = 11.11 + 109.65 = 120.76 MPa tension.
Outer fibre, r = 100 mm: σ<sub>b</sub> = 1,400,000 × (65.48 − 100) / (1800 × 4.52 × 100) = −59.42 MPa. Total σ<sub>outer</sub> = 11.11 − 59.42 = −48.31 MPa, i.e. 48.31 MPa compression.
examples.answer: Maximum tensile stress is 120.8 MPa at the inner fibre; outer-fibre stress is −48.3 MPa, i.e. 48.3 MPa compression.
examples.check:
import math
P = 20000.0
b = 30.0
h = 60.0
Ri = 40.0
Ro = Ri + h
A = b * h
R = Ri + h / 2
Rn = h / math.log(Ro / Ri)
e = R - Rn
M = P * R
sigma_i = P / A + M * (Rn - Ri) / (A * e * Ri)
sigma_o = P / A + M * (Rn - Ro) / (A * e * Ro)
print(round(sigma_i, 1))
print(round(sigma_o, 1))

code.code:
import math
P = 20000.0
b = 30.0
h = 60.0
Ri = 40.0
Ro = Ri + h
A = b * h
R = Ri + h / 2
Rn = h / math.log(Ro / Ri)
e = R - Rn
M = P * R
print(round(P / A + M * (Rn - Ri) / (A * e * Ri), 1))
print(round(P / A + M * (Rn - Ro) / (A * e * Ro), 1))

traps: Using σ = My/I for a deeply curved member: it under-predicts the inner-fibre stress. Use the curved-beam formula when h is not small compared with R.
Putting R instead of R<sub>n</sub> in the stress formula, or forgetting e = R − R<sub>n</sub>.
Forgetting direct stress P/A, or adding it with the wrong sign. In a crane hook under opening load, direct stress is tensile at both fibres.
Using diameter instead of radius, or mixing N·mm with m. Keep every length in mm so stress comes out in MPa.
Treating the inner fibre as compressive for a crane hook. Opening the hook puts the inner fibre in tension; the outer fibre is compressed.

quiz.q: Write the neutral-axis radius R<sub>n</sub> for a rectangular curved beam of depth h, inner radius R<sub>i</sub> and outer radius R<sub>o</sub>.
Why is the inner-fibre bending stress higher than the outer-fibre stress in a curved beam?
quiz.a: The neutral axis shifts toward the centre of curvature. The inner fibre has a smaller radius r, so the term (R<sub>n</sub> − r)/(e r) is largest there. Strain is not linear in r, and the small denominator raises the stress.

quiz.q: A curved beam has R<sub>n</sub> = 50 mm, e = 2 mm, A = 300 mm² and M = 60,000 N·mm. Find the bending stress at r = 40 mm.
A rectangular curved beam has b = 20 mm, h = 40 mm, R<sub>i</sub> = 20 mm and R<sub>o</sub> = 60 mm. Find R<sub>n</sub> and e.
A hook has h/R = 0.8. A student uses the straight-beam formula. Is the design safe on the inner fibre? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. With h/R = 0.8, curvature is strong. The straight-beam formula under-predicts the inner-fibre stress, so the design is unsafe even if the straight calculation passes.

quiz.q: In a crane hook under opening load, which fibre carries the maximum compressive stress?
quiz.a: The outer fibre. Bending gives compression there, and direct tension P/A reduces the compressive magnitude. The inner fibre is in tension.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real hook design uses standard hook profiles, proof-load tests and finite-element analysis. The classical curved-beam result is often called the Winkler–Bach formula. Search next for 'Winkler-Bach curved beam', 'crane hook stress analysis' and 'C-frame press frame design'.
